content_html:
You walk into the mosque on Friday and the imam is already on the minbar giving the khutbah (Friday sermon). Do you sit straight down to listen, or do you pray tahiyyat al-masjid during the khutbah (the two-rak'ah prayer of greeting the mosque)? The answer shown by the explicit Sunnah is: pray two light rak'ahs, then sit. The Prophet ﷺ commanded exactly this to a man who came in while he was speaking. In this article we give the hadith of Sulayk al-Ghatafani in its wording from Bukhari and Muslim, the views of the schools of fiqh, how to pray the two rak'ahs, and then the etiquette of listening to the khutbah and what cancels the special reward of Jummah.

Do you pray tahiyyat al-masjid while the imam is giving the khutbah?

Yes. Whoever enters the mosque on Friday while the imam is giving the khutbah prays two light rak'ahs and then sits. This is the view of the Shafi'is and Hanbalis, based on the Prophet's words ﷺ to Sulayk al-Ghatafani: "O Sulayk, stand and pray two rak'ahs, and keep them short" (Sahih Muslim 875). The Hanafis and Malikis hold that he should sit and listen, but the first view has the more explicit evidence.

Tahiyyat al-masjid is in principle an emphasised sunnah at any time, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "When one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before he sits." (Sahih al-Bukhari 444, Sahih Muslim 714) The question here is whether the time of the khutbah is an exception, given that listening to the khutbah is obligatory. This is where the hadith of Sulayk comes as a clear text on the issue.

The hadith of Sulayk al-Ghatafani in Bukhari and Muslim

The wording in Sahih Muslim

Jabir ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said:

"Sulayk al-Ghatafani came on Friday while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was giving the khutbah, and he sat down. So he said to him: 'O Sulayk, stand and pray two rak'ahs, and keep them short.' Then he said: 'When one of you comes on Friday while the imam is giving the khutbah, let him pray two rak'ahs and keep them short.'" (Sahih Muslim 875)

The wording in Sahih al-Bukhari

Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) also said: a man came while the Prophet ﷺ was addressing the people on Friday, and he said, "Have you prayed, O so-and-so?" He said, "No." He said, "Stand and pray." (Sahih al-Bukhari 930) And in another place in Sahih al-Bukhari, Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ said while giving the khutbah:

"When one of you comes while the imam is giving the khutbah, or has come out [for it], let him pray two rak'ahs." (Sahih al-Bukhari 1166)

As for some narrations in which he asked, "Did you pray two rak'ahs before you came?", al-Albani judged the addition "before you came" to be shadh (an irregular narration that contradicts more reliable ones), so it cannot be used as evidence that a sunnah prayer before Jummah is meant.

What do we learn from the hadith?

  • It is a general verbal command, not a single action: "When one of you comes...", so it cannot be restricted to the case of Sulayk alone.
  • The Prophet ﷺ interrupted his khutbah to tell him to pray, which shows how emphasised it is in this situation.
  • Keeping it short is intended: "keep them short" means make them light, so he can turn to listening.
  • Whoever sits down out of ignorance or forgetfulness stands up and prays them: Sulayk sat and was then told to stand, so the prayer is not lost by sitting briefly.
  • The imam may speak to someone in the congregation during the khutbah for a good reason, and that person may answer him.

What do the jurists say about tahiyyat al-masjid during the khutbah?

ViewWho held itMain evidence
He prays two light rak'ahs and then sitsThe Shafi'is, the Hanbalis and the people of hadith; preferred by Ibn Baz and Ibn UthayminThe hadith of Sulayk in Muslim (875) and al-Bukhari (930, 1166)
He sits without praying and listens to the khutbahThe Hanafis and Malikis; al-Qadi Iyad reported it from the majority of the early generationsThe command to listen in silence, and his words ﷺ to a man stepping over people's necks: "Sit down, for you have caused harm"

The evidence of the Hanafis and Malikis, and the response

Those who held that one should not pray cited Allah's words:

﴿وَإِذَا قُرِئَ الْقُرْآنُ فَاسْتَمِعُوا لَهُ وَأَنصِتُوا لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ﴾ "So when the Qur'ān is recited, then listen to it and pay attention that you may receive mercy." (Surah Al-A'raf 7:204, translation: Sahih International)

They also cited the hadith commanding silence on Friday, and the hadith of Abdullah ibn Busr (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man came stepping over people's necks on Friday while the Prophet ﷺ was giving the khutbah, and he said to him: "Sit down, for you have caused harm." (Sunan Abi Dawud 1118, graded sahih by al-Albani) He told him to sit and did not tell him to pray. They also cited a hadith attributed to the Prophet: "When one of you enters the mosque while the imam is on the minbar, there is no prayer and no talking until the imam finishes." This hadith is not authentic: at-Tabarani narrated it with a chain containing an abandoned (matruk) narrator, al-Albani judged it false in his Silsilat al-Ahadith ad-Da'ifah (87), and al-Bayhaqi said that attributing it to the Prophet is a mistake.

Those who hold that one should pray replied that the hadith of Sulayk is a specific text on this very issue, and a specific text takes precedence over a general one. As for "Sit down, for you have caused harm", its purpose was to stop him stepping over people; it is possible the man had already prayed, or that he was told to sit in his place and then pray, and an explicit text is not abandoned because of a mere possibility. That is why Shaykh Ibn Baz said in his fatwa on tahiyyat al-masjid during the khutbah (Arabic) that the Prophet's command is explicit and that the Sunnah comes before anyone's opinion. Still, whoever follows the Hanafi or Maliki school, following the scholars of his country, should not be harshly criticised, because this is a matter of difference between the imams.

How do you pray tahiyyat al-masjid while the imam is giving the khutbah?

  1. Enter calmly and sit in the nearest empty space; do not step over people's necks.
  2. Pray two rak'ahs before you sit; if you sat down forgetfully, stand up and pray them.
  3. Keep them light: recite Al-Fatihah and a short surah or a few verses, and keep the ruku' (bowing) and sujud (prostration) short while still being calm and settled in them.
  4. Do not pray more than two rak'ahs; what is commanded is only two light rak'ahs.
  5. Sit straight after them and listen to the khutbah; do not busy yourself with audible dhikr or recitation.
  6. If you enter as the iqamah is being called, do not start the tahiyyah; join the imam in the obligatory prayer.

A related question: if you enter while the muezzin is calling the adhan given in front of the khatib, some scholars held that you should pray the tahiyyah at that point so you are free to hear the khutbah from its beginning, because listening to the khutbah is obligatory while repeating after the muezzin is sunnah. The khatib himself does not pray tahiyyat al-masjid when he enters for the khutbah; he goes straight up the minbar, as the Prophet ﷺ used to do.

Etiquette of listening to the Friday khutbah: what is allowed and what is not

Listening to the khutbah in silence is obligatory according to the majority of scholars, and there are explicit hadith on it. Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"If you say to your companion on Friday, 'Be quiet', while the imam is giving the khutbah, you have engaged in idle talk (laghw)." (Sahih al-Bukhari 934, Sahih Muslim 851)

If saying "be quiet", which is itself enjoining good, counts as idle talk, then other speech is even more clearly forbidden. Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) also reported that the Prophet ﷺ said:

"Whoever makes wudu and does it well, then comes to Jumu'ah, listens and is silent, is forgiven what is between that and the next Jumu'ah, plus three more days. And whoever touches pebbles has engaged in idle talk." (Sahih Muslim 857)

"Idle talk" (laghw) here means something that reduces the special reward of Jummah, although the prayer itself is valid. Here is a table of the things people most often ask about during the khutbah:

Action during the khutbahRulingNote
Talking to the person next to you, even to say "be quiet"Not allowed"You have engaged in idle talk" (Bukhari 934, Muslim 851)
Fiddling with pebbles, the carpet or prayer beadsNot allowed"Whoever touches pebbles has engaged in idle talk" (Muslim 857)
Browsing your phone or replying to messagesNot allowedIt distracts the heart more than touching pebbles
Gesturing to someone talking to be quietAllowed according to many scholarsInstead of speaking
Sending blessings on the Prophet ﷺ and saying Ameen to the du'aAllowed, silentlyWithout raising your voice and disturbing others
Returning a salam or responding to someone who sneezesDisputed; the more cautious course is not to do either out loudWhoever sneezes praises Allah within himself
Speaking with the khatib for a need, or answering his questionAllowedLike the exchange with Sulayk, and the Bedouin asking for rain (Bukhari 933, Muslim 897)
Stepping over people's necksProhibited"Sit down, for you have caused harm" (Abu Dawud 1118, graded sahih by al-Albani)

Good manners also include putting your phone on silent before entering the mosque, sitting close to the imam, and going early to Jummah, because most of these problems never arise for someone who arrives before the imam climbs the minbar. You will find the rest of the day's etiquette in the sunnahs of Jummah.

Do you pray tahiyyat al-masjid if you enter at the zenith on Friday?

Your arrival may coincide with the time when the sun is at its zenith just before it declines, which is one of the times in which prayer is forbidden on days other than Friday. Those who hold that tahiyyat al-masjid is prayed during the khutbah hold that it can be prayed at any time anyway, because it is a prayer with a specific reason. The Shafi'is held that voluntary prayer is not disliked at the zenith on Friday at all. As for the khutbah, it is usually after the sun has passed the zenith, so the two issues do not arise together. The zenith time itself differs from city to city, as we explained in prayer times calculation methods. The details of the forbidden times and the ruling on prayers with a reason in them are in forbidden times for prayer.

Common mistakes when entering the mosque during the khutbah

  • Making the two rak'ahs long: some people pray them like a night prayer, when what is commanded is to keep them short.
  • Praying four rak'ahs or more: intending a sunnah before Jummah, when what is prescribed during the khutbah is two rak'ahs only.
  • Stepping over the rows to reach the front row while the khutbah is under way, which is a prohibited form of harm.
  • Criticising someone who prays the tahiyyah, or someone who sits following his school, when this is a matter of difference between the imams.
  • Greeting those sitting with an audible salam during the khutbah, which forces them to reply or puts them in an awkward position.
  • Reading Surah Al-Kahf during the khutbah: its time is before the khutbah or after the prayer. Its virtue is explained in reading Surah Al-Kahf on Friday.

Summary: pray two light rak'ahs, then listen

Whoever enters the mosque on Friday while the imam is giving the khutbah prays two light rak'ahs and then sits, acting on the Prophet's command ﷺ to Sulayk al-Ghatafani in Sahih Muslim and on his general statement in Sahih al-Bukhari: "When one of you comes while the imam is giving the khutbah, or has come out, let him pray two rak'ahs." This is the view of the Shafi'is and Hanbalis; the Hanafis and Malikis differed and held that one should sit and listen. After that, listening in silence to the khutbah is obligatory: no talking and no fidgeting; even saying "be quiet" counts as idle talk. Make a point of going early, because it spares you most of these questions and puts you in the best hours of Jummah, and learn about the hour of acceptance on Friday. What we have presented is a summary of the scholars' views; for specific questions, it is best to ask the scholars in your country.

faq.q: I came in during the khutbah and sat down. Should I stand up to pray the tahiyyah?
faq.a: Yes. If you sat down forgetfully or not knowing the ruling and only sat briefly, stand and pray two light rak'ahs. Sulayk al-Ghatafani sat down and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "O Sulayk, stand and pray two rak'ahs, and keep them short" (Muslim). Sitting briefly does not cancel the tahiyyah, but if you have sat for a long time, many scholars hold that its moment has passed.

faq.q: What does "keep them short" mean in the hadith?
faq.a: It means make them light and limit yourself to the minimum that completes the prayer while staying calm in each position: for example, recite Al-Fatihah and a few verses or a short surah, and keep the bowing, prostration and tashahhud brief, so you can quickly turn to the obligatory listening. Keeping them short is intended by the Shariah, not merely a concession; making them long goes against the Prophet's command.

faq.q: Why do the Malikis not pray tahiyyat al-masjid during the khutbah?
faq.a: The Malikis and Hanafis hold that listening to the khutbah is obligatory and that praying distracts from it. They cite the command to be silent and the hadith "Sit down, for you have caused harm" said to a man stepping over people. The Shafi'is and Hanbalis hold that the hadith of Sulayk is a specific, explicit text that takes precedence. It is a matter of difference among the four imams, and someone following the school of his country's scholars should not be criticised.

faq.q: Is the hadith "When the imam ascends the minbar there is no prayer and no talking" authentic?
faq.a: It is not authentic as a saying of the Prophet ﷺ. At-Tabarani narrated it with a chain containing an abandoned narrator, al-Albani judged it false in Silsilat ad-Da'ifah, and al-Bayhaqi said attributing it to the Prophet is a mistake. What is established in Bukhari and Muslim is the command to listen in silence to the khutbah, and the command to pray two light rak'ahs for whoever enters while the imam is speaking, so the authentic is not opposed by what is not established.

faq.q: Can I return a salam or respond to someone who sneezes during the khutbah?
faq.a: Scholars differ on this. The more cautious course is not to reply out loud, because even saying "be quiet" was counted as idle talk in the agreed-upon hadith; you may reply with a gesture. Whoever sneezes during the khutbah praises Allah within himself without raising his voice, those around him do not respond aloud, and the salam can be returned after the khutbah if you wish.

faq.q: Do I pray a sunnah before Jummah if I enter while the imam is giving the khutbah?
faq.a: No. What is prescribed for someone who enters during the khutbah is only two light rak'ahs and then sitting; he should not add more with the intention of a sunnah before Jummah or anything else. In the narration containing "Did you pray before you came?", al-Albani judged the addition "before you came" to be irregular (shadh), so it is not evidence for a sunnah before Jummah. The tahiyyah suffices in this situation.

faq.q: Does talking during the khutbah cancel the reward of Jummah?
faq.a: Your prayer is valid, but talking during the khutbah is idle talk that reduces the special reward of Jummah, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "If you say to your companion 'Be quiet' while the imam is giving the khutbah, you have engaged in idle talk" (agreed upon), and "Whoever touches pebbles has engaged in idle talk" (Muslim). So make sure to listen in silence from the start of the khutbah to its end.
